lead: Nadifloxacin is a topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for acne vulgaris and for bacterial skin infections. For appearance, it is used to calm inflamed pimples and pustules so the skin looks clearer and less red, often alongside a retinoid such as adapalene or with benzoyl peroxide.[1][2][3]

It is marketed as a 1% cream in Japan, parts of Europe and some Asian countries, and is not approved in the United States.[1][2] It works by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and is active in vitro against Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), Staphylococcus epidermidis and MRSA.[2]

Randomised trials in Japanese, Korean and other Asian patients report lesion reductions with nadifloxacin 1%, including a split-face trial against vehicle, a comparison with erythromycin gel, and a combination study with adapalene.[4][5][6] Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolone use could promote quinolone resistance.[2]

angle.text: Patients use the cream to reduce inflammatory acne lesions. Dermatologists in countries where it is sold prescribe it on its own or combined with adapalene or benzoyl peroxide to clear inflamed spots faster.

paras: Nadifloxacin is used for mild to moderate acne, where it targets the inflamed papules and pustules that drive redness and visible blemishes.[1][2] Grokipedia says it is often combined with benzoyl peroxide or adapalene.[1]
It is also used for pyodermas such as impetigo and folliculitis.[1][2] A small study in young children examined it for atopic dermatitis complicated by MRSA.[7]

A randomised split-face trial in Korean patients with mild to moderate acne found inflammatory lesions fell by about 70 percent on the nadifloxacin-treated side while rising on the vehicle side, with histology showing reduced inflammation.[5]
A randomised comparison of 86 patients found nadifloxacin 1% cream and erythromycin 4% gel both reduced lesion counts and severity scores from week 4 through 12 weeks, with similar results.[4]

In a 12-week multicentre Japanese trial of 184 patients with moderate-to-severe acne, adding nadifloxacin 1% cream to adapalene 0.1% gel reduced inflammatory lesions significantly more than adapalene alone from week 4, and none of the 76 tested bacterial strains was resistant to nadifloxacin.[6]

Adverse reactions are mostly local: burning, itching (most common), contact dermatitis, dryness and irritation.[2] A 21-day patch study in 40 healthy volunteers found that nadifloxacin combined with adapalene, benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid or isotretinoin produced mostly zero irritation scores, all below 1.[8]

Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolone use could promote quinolone resistance.[2] Studies of acne bacteria have documented resistance to other topical antibiotics such as erythromycin and clindamycin in several countries.[9]

It inhibits DNA gyrase, halting bacterial replication, and may have sebostatic and anti-inflammatory effects.[2] After a single large application of 1% cream, peak plasma level was 107 ng/mL with a half-life of 19.4 hours.[2]
It is a racemic fluoroquinolone, formula C19H21FN2O4, molar mass about 360.4 g/mol.[2]

Randomised trials include a split-face versus vehicle study in Korea,[5] a comparison with erythromycin gel,[4] a Japanese multicentre trial of nadifloxacin plus adapalene versus adapalene,[6] and an irritation study of combinations.[8] Grokipedia (AI-generated, less reliable) also describes comparisons with clindamycin combinations.[1] A registered phase 4 trial comparing nadifloxacin plus tretinoin with clindamycin plus tretinoin for mild-to-moderate acne is recruiting.[3]

name: Nadifloxacin

card.summary: A topical quinolone antibiotic cream for acne used in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia but not the US.
card.note: Not US-approved; concern about quinolone resistance.

quick.overview:
Nadifloxacin is a 1% antibiotic cream for acne and skin infections, available in Japan, some European and Asian countries.

Small studies reportedly show lesion reductions comparable to clindamycin combinations, but evidence in the sources is limited.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, killing or stopping acne-related bacteria such as Cutibacterium acnes, and may have anti-inflammatory effects.
quick.risks: Mostly local burning, itching, dryness. Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolones could promote resistance. Not approved in the US.
